case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance standard for permanent-neglect terminations violated the Due Process Clause and that a State must support its allegations at a parental-rights termination proceeding by at least clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: The federal source of Idaho's clear-and-convincing burden under I.C. § 16-2005, applied in every Idaho termination appeal in this set.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not require appointed counsel for every indigent parent in a termination proceeding and left the appointment question to the trial court in the first instance, subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the federal constitutional minimum for counsel in termination cases; Idaho's statutory right to counsel in Title 16 proceedings is more protective than this floor.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

key_cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of Doe (2014-09)
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a stepparent-adoption termination petition, holding that although abandonment was proved, the petitioners failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that termination was in the children's best interests and that a stepparent's superior parenting cannot be the basis for termination.
key_cases.relevance: The leading recent Idaho statement that best interests is an independent clear-and-convincing element in every termination case.
key_cases.quote: The magistrate court correctly held that the decision to terminate a parent's parental rights cannot be based upon whether a stepparent would better fulfill parental responsibilities than the biological parent

key_cases.case_name: In re Termination of the Parental Rights of John Doe (2014-26)
key_cases.holding: The court vacated a termination judgment that rested solely on a murder conviction and sentence later vacated on appeal, and construed I.C. § 16-2005(1)(e) to require that the parent be serving a sentence and be likely to remain incarcerated for a substantial period of the child's remaining minority.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Idaho construction of the incarcerated-parent ground, including the factors a court may weigh in measuring a substantial period.
key_cases.quote: In context, the word "incarcerated" refers to someone who has been convicted of a crime and is serving a sentence of incarceration

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Department of Health & Welfare v. Hays
key_cases.holding: Affirming the district court's reversal of the magistrate, the court held that where parental rights have been terminated and the Department is appointed guardian of the child's person, the Department alone must consent to an adoption and therefore alone selects the adoptive parents, subject only to the adoption court's power to deny a petition that is not in the children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: The originating Idaho holding that the Department alone consents to, and therefore selects, the adoptive parents for a child in its guardianship — the rule In re Adoption of John Doe later applies.
key_cases.quote: The authority to consent to the adoption of a child necessarily includes the authority to decide who can be the adoptive parents.

key_cases.case_name: Idaho Dep't of Health & Welfare v. Doe (In Re Doe)
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that substantial and competent evidence supported the magistrate's findings that the mother neglected her three children under both I.C. §§ 16-1602(31) and 16-2002(3)(b) and that termination was in the children's best interests, restating that due process requires the State to prove a statutory ground and best interests by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: The current Idaho articulation of what the State must prove to terminate, quoted in later decisions including IDHW v. John Doe (2023-25).
key_cases.quote: a parent-child relationship may be terminated if the parent has neglected the child and it is in the child's best interest to terminate the relationship
